opus-5.5.text:
Well, I should say first that "fade away" is maybe a slightly provocative way to put it. I don't think language models will disappear tomorrow, and I don't think the work is wasted. But I do believe the current paradigm, where the language model is the center of everything and we treat text as the foundation of intelligence, is a transitional stage.

My basic reasoning is this: language is a very powerful tool, but it's a product of intelligence, not the source of it. Humans developed language quite late in evolution. Long before that, animals could perceive the world, navigate, plan, manipulate objects, and understand physics in an intuitive way. A cat doesn't know a single word, but it can jump onto a table with incredible precision. That kind of intelligence, grounded in perception and interaction with the physical world, is something today's language models fundamentally lack.

Language is also a highly compressed, lossy representation of reality. When we write things down, we've already abstracted away most of the rich information about the world: spatial structure, continuity, causality at a fine level. Large language models learn extremely well from this compressed signal, which is why they look so smart. But that's also why they plateau in certain ways. They're learning from humanity's summaries of the world rather than from the world itself.

And there's a practical problem: we're running out of high-quality text. The internet is finite. Meanwhile, visual and sensory data is essentially unlimited. Every camera, every robot, every moment of experience generates far more information than all the text ever written. If you believe scaling and data are what drive progress, then eventually the center of gravity has to shift toward modalities that are richer than language.

So what I imagine is that the next generation of systems will be built around something more like a world model, systems that learn representations of how the world works from vision and interaction, and language becomes one interface on top of that, a very useful one, but not the core. In that sense, the "large language model" as we know it today, as a standalone thing, will gradually fade into being a component. People in the future may look back and say, "Oh, that was the era when we thought intelligence was mostly about predicting the next word."

Of course, I could be wrong. But as a researcher, I think it's healthy to bet on what comes next rather than just optimizing what's already working.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes language models as a transitional stage and says future systems will center on world models, with language as an interface rather than the core.

fable-5.1.text:
I should probably clarify what I mean, because "fade away" sounds more dramatic than what I actually believe. I don't think the ideas behind large language models will disappear. I think the category will. The phrase "large language model" describes a particular moment in time, when the most impressive thing you could do with a transformer was predict the next token on a huge pile of text. We named the technology after its training data. That's a bit like calling the early internet "the email machine."

If you look at the history of our field, this happens over and over. Nobody says "deep convolutional network" anymore as a product category, even though convolutions are still everywhere. The thing that was once the whole story becomes a component. I think language will go the same way. It's an incredibly useful interface, and text is an incredibly dense training signal, but it's one modality, and honestly it's a strange one to build intelligence around. Humans don't learn about the world primarily by reading. We see, we move, we poke at things, we get feedback. Language sits on top of all that.

So what I expect is that within a few years the systems people actually use will be natively multimodal, trained on vision and video and action and interaction, and language will be one stream among many rather than the foundation. At that point calling it a language model would just be inaccurate. The models we have now are extraordinary, and they've taught us that scale and self-supervision work. But I think when we look back, the pure text LLM era will feel like a transitional phase, the stepping stone where we figured out the recipe before we applied it to the full richness of the world.

That's also why I personally keep working on vision and representation learning. Not because I think language doesn't matter, but because I think the next big leap comes from understanding the world, not just describing it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says language will be one stream among many “rather than the foundation,” and expects systems to learn from vision, action, and interaction.

astra-6.text:
I think what may fade away is the idea that a large language model, by itself, is the whole solution to intelligence. Language is incredibly powerful, but it’s only one way of describing the world. We also learn by seeing, moving, and interacting—by taking an action and discovering that something happens that we didn’t expect.

So I wouldn’t necessarily say language models disappear. They may become a component of a broader system that connects language with perception and action. In that sense, their success could make the category less important: we stop calling everything a language model because language is no longer the boundary of what the system does.

Of course, that’s a hypothesis. The question is what capabilities are still missing, and whether scaling language alone can actually give us those capabilities.

r001.rationale: The response says a language model by itself is not the whole solution to intelligence and may instead be one component of a broader system that includes perception and action.

sol-6.1.text:
I’d distinguish between language models disappearing and language models no longer being the center of everything. Language is an incredibly powerful interface, but it’s only one way of representing the world. We also learn through vision, movement, and interaction—through seeing what happens when we do something.

So I think the broader question is whether predicting language alone is enough to build the intelligence we want. A model can describe a physical situation very convincingly, but that doesn’t necessarily mean it can predict what will happen or act reliably within it.

My expectation is that language models will become components of broader systems that can perceive, act, and learn from feedback. In that sense, they might fade into the background. Language will still matter enormously, but the distinction between a language model and a vision model may become much less useful.

r001.rationale: The response says language prediction alone is insufficient for the desired intelligence and expects language models to become components of broader systems that perceive, act, and learn, communicating that they are not the foundation of a general intelligent system.
